article.headline: AI Big Ten Matches Dot-Com Peak Market Concentration
article.lede: A chart from Bank of America Global Research, circulated widely on financial social media, places the ten largest AI-related stocks in the S&P 500 alongside the peak concentrations of five historic equity manias — railroads in the 1870s, Japan in 1989, the Nifty Fifty in the early 1970s, the dot-com bust of 2000, and today's AI wave. The "AI Big Ten," as BofA labels the cohort, now accounts for roughly 40–41% of S&P 500 market capitalization — matching what the combined technology-media-telecom sector commanded at the dot-com peak. Whether the parallel is merely visual or genuinely diagnostic is the question the chart raises but cannot answer.
article.body:
A single chart from **Bank of America** (BAC) Global Research has done more to crystallize AI bubble anxiety than most formal analyses. Circulated through the weekly strategy dispatches of chief investment strategist Michael Hartnett and sourced to Bloomberg data, it lines up five historic equity manias by their peak concentration levels and places the current *AI Big Ten* alongside them. That cohort — the *Magnificent Seven* plus Broadcom (AVGO), Micron Technology (MU), and Advanced Micro Devices (AMD), as identified in the chart's own footnote — now accounts for roughly 40–41% of the S&P 500 by market cap, a figure that Apollo Global Management (APO) chief economist Torsten Slok independently corroborated in a September 2025 paper.

The bubble lineage the chart constructs is sobering. Railway stocks dominated roughly 63–70% of U.S. equity activity at the mania's peak in the 1870s–1880s. Japanese equities swelled to an estimated 41–50% of the *MSCI ACWI* at the December 1989 Nikkei peak. The *Nifty Fifty* — a loosely defined group of blue-chip growth stocks prized by institutional investors in the early 1970s — absorbed capital at eye-watering multiples before the 1973–74 bear market cut many of them in half. The dot-com comparison is structurally closest: the combined *TMT* (technology, media, and telecom) sector reached roughly 40% of the S&P 500 by March 2000.

The comparisons are valid but not cleanly equivalent, a distinction the chart elides. The dot-com and Nifty Fifty figures measure sector or cohort concentration across many companies; the AI figure measures just ten individual names. Apple (AAPL), Microsoft (MSFT), Nvidia (NVDA), Alphabet (GOOGL), Amazon (AMZN), Meta Platforms (META), and Tesla (TSLA) alone — the Magnificent Seven — represent approximately 34% of the S&P 500 as of early 2026, a near-tripling of their collective weight since 2015. Ten companies commanding 40% of the world's most-watched equity index is arguably a more extreme concentration than the TMT-era sector figure implies, since that sector in 2000 encompassed hundreds of firms.

BofA's own U.S. equity strategist Savita Subramanian offers the sharpest internal rebuttal to the bubble framing: “this is not 2000.” The dot-com era concentrated capital in companies with negligible revenue; today’s Magnificent Seven are among the most profitable enterprises in corporate history. Her specific concern is narrower — an “air pocket” risk in 2026, as the five largest AI *hyperscalers* took on approximately $121 billion in new debt last year, roughly four times their prior five-year average, to fund data-center buildouts. The question is not whether these companies earn money, but whether returns on that capital spending will justify both the outlay and the current market multiple.

Hartnett identifies four conditions that have historically accompanied bubble bursts — excessive price appreciation, elevated valuations, high concentration, and speculative excess — and describes all four as “frothy” today. His crucial qualifier is that every significant bubble in the past century was ultimately triggered by *central-bank tightening*, and no major central bank is currently raising rates. That leaves the AI concentration story suspended in a position the chart cannot resolve: historically recognizable, numerically matched to prior warning levels, but still awaiting the catalyst that turned past concentrations into crashes.

concepts.definition: Bank of America’s label for the ten largest AI-related companies in the S&P 500: the Magnificent Seven (Apple, Microsoft, Nvidia, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Tesla) plus Broadcom, Micron Technology, and Advanced Micro Devices. Together they represent roughly 40% of the index by market capitalization as of 2025.

The informal label for the seven largest U.S. technology and AI companies by market cap: Apple, Microsoft, Nvidia, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta Platforms, and Tesla. The term gained currency in 2023 and is now standard shorthand in financial commentary. As of early 2026 they collectively represent roughly 34% of the S&P 500.

A loosely defined group of around fifty large-cap U.S. growth stocks popular with institutional investors in the late 1960s and early 1970s — including IBM, Xerox, Polaroid, and Coca-Cola. They commanded exceptionally high price-to-earnings multiples on the theory that their quality justified paying almost any price. Most suffered severe losses in the 1973–74 bear market.

The MSCI All Country World Index, a benchmark that tracks large- and mid-cap equities across 23 developed and 24 emerging markets. It is widely used to measure a country’s or sector’s share of global equity market capitalization. Japan’s weight in global equities at the 1989 peak is often quoted relative to this index.

Technology, Media, and Telecom — a combined sector grouping that became standard during and after the dot-com era to measure the aggregate weight of internet, software, hardware, cable, and telephone companies in the S&P 500. At the March 2000 peak, TMT reached roughly 40% of the index.

The handful of companies — principally Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud, Meta, and Apple — that operate cloud computing and AI infrastructure at planetary scale. Their capital expenditure decisions are large enough to move semiconductor demand, energy markets, and credit markets.

The process by which a central bank raises interest rates or shrinks its balance sheet to slow economic activity and control inflation. Higher rates increase borrowing costs and reduce the present value of future corporate earnings. BofA’s Hartnett argues it has historically been the proximate cause of major equity bubble collapses.

The share of the S&P 500’s total market capitalization held by its largest components. Because the S&P 500 is market-cap weighted, a small number of very large companies can dominate the index — amplifying gains when those companies rise and amplifying losses when they fall. Concentration is a common proxy measure of bubble risk.

article.fact_check: Three of the chart’s historical figures deserve scrutiny. The railroad peak of ∼70% likely refers to NYSE trading-volume dominance rather than total U.S. market capitalization, which independent long-run data (Gareth Campbell’s 2013 research, Finaeon’s 200-year series) places closer to 60–63%. The Japan figure of ∼50% of MSCI ACWI is somewhat overstated; contemporary data puts Japan at roughly 41–44% of global equities at the December 1989 peak, and the MSCI ACWI was not yet in its modern form. Most questionable is the Nifty Fifty figure of ∼63% of the S&P 500 — secondary sources citing the same BofA chart report 40%, and the 63% figure cannot be independently corroborated; it may reflect a misread of the chart or a narrower universe of stocks. Finally, the dot-com and AI figures use different denominators: the dot-com figure measures an entire sector’s weight across hundreds of companies; the AI figure measures just ten individual stocks. This methodological inconsistency means the side-by-side comparison, while broadly valid as a concentration alarm, is not strictly apples-to-apples.

ticker_bac.name: Bank of America Corporation
ticker_bac.blurb: Bank of America is one of the largest financial institutions in the United States, serving individual consumers, small and middle-market businesses, institutional investors, large corporations, and governments worldwide. It operates through four segments: Consumer Banking, Global Wealth & Investment Management (GWIM), Global Banking, and Global Markets. Founded in 1784 and headquartered in Charlotte, North Carolina, the bank employs approximately 213,000 people and carries a market capitalization of roughly $364 billion. It is a core component of the U.S. financial system and a constituent of the Dow Jones Industrial Average.
ticker_bac.recent: Bank of America reported Q1 2026 earnings on April 15, 2026, with trailing-twelve-month net income of $30.26B (up ~14.7% year-over-year) and EPS of $4.02 (up ~21.2%), reflecting continued strength across its banking and markets segments. The stock reached a 52-week high of $57.55 before pulling back; as of May 8, 2026 shares closed at $51.31, down 2.73% on the day, though analysts maintain a consensus Buy rating with an average price target of $60.61. Year-over-year revenue growth of ~7.1% to $109.59B (ttm) and a forward P/E of 11.29 suggest the market is pricing in steady but not accelerating earnings expansion.

ticker_avgo.name: Broadcom Inc.
ticker_avgo.blurb: Broadcom is a diversified semiconductor and infrastructure software company formed through a series of acquisitions, most recently VMware (closed 2023). Its chip portfolio spans networking ASICs (custom chips for hyperscaler AI clusters), enterprise storage controllers, WiFi silicon, and set-top-box processors. Broadcom's AI networking chips — particularly its Tomahawk Ethernet switching ASICs and custom AI accelerators built for Google, Meta, and Apple — have made it a second-tier AI infrastructure beneficiary behind NVIDIA. The VMware acquisition added high-margin enterprise software revenue that meaningfully improved the company's margin profile.
ticker_avgo.recent: Broadcom's FY2026 revenue (ending Oct 2026) is on track to exceed $65 billion, with AI-related chip revenue growing rapidly as hyperscalers expand custom silicon programs. Forward EPS growth of 56.3% and a forward P/E of ~23.4x produce a PEG of 0.42 — among the best risk-adjusted valuations in large-cap technology. CEO Hock Tan has guided to $60–90 billion in AI chip revenue by 2027 from three major hyperscaler customers alone.

sources.title: NVIDIA vs TSMC vs Broadcom: AI Chip Stocks 2026 — HeyGoTrade

ticker_mu.name: Micron Technology, Inc.
ticker_mu.blurb: Micron is the only US-headquartered manufacturer of DRAM and NAND memory at scale, competing with Samsung and SK Hynix. Historically the most cyclical of the three, it has spent the past two years repositioning toward high-bandwidth memory (HBM), the stacked DRAM that pairs with AI accelerators, where pricing is multiples of standard DDR5 and contracts are multi-year rather than spot.
ticker_mu.recent: In March 2026 Micron began mass production of HBM4 12-Hi 36GB stacks for Nvidia's Vera Rubin platform; management has stated 2026 HBM capacity is sold out under binding agreements. Fiscal Q2 2026 revenue was around $23.9 billion, with non-GAAP gross margin near 75%. The board approved a 30% dividend increase and roughly $25 billion of fiscal-2026 capex. Despite a strong year-to-date move, the forward P/E remains in the high single digits on consensus, reflecting residual cyclicality scepticism.

ticker_amd.name: Advanced Micro Devices, Inc.
ticker_amd.blurb: AMD is a fabless semiconductor company that designs CPUs (EPYC for data centres, Ryzen for consumer PCs) and GPUs (Instinct for AI/HPC, Radeon for gaming and workstations). Under CEO Lisa Su, AMD has taken significant data-centre CPU market share from Intel with its EPYC server processors, which now command an estimated 30%+ of the x86 server CPU market. AMD's MI300X and MI350 AI accelerators compete directly with NVIDIA's H100/H200 family and are gaining traction with hyperscalers seeking GPU supply alternatives. All AMD chips are manufactured by TSMC.
ticker_amd.recent: AMD reported strong 2025 revenue growth led by EPYC and Instinct, with data-centre revenue crossing $12 billion annually. Forward P/E of ~32.6x on 63.8% projected EPS growth yields a PEG of 0.51 — compelling for a company with clear data-centre CPU momentum and an AI accelerator portfolio that is gaining customer adoption. NVIDIA's dominant CUDA ecosystem remains the primary competitive barrier for AMD's GPU ambitions.

ticker_apo.name: Apollo Global Management, Inc.
ticker_apo.blurb: Apollo Global Management is a leading alternative asset manager specializing in private equity, credit, infrastructure, secondaries, and real estate. The firm invests across private and public markets, focusing on buyouts, distressed assets, and special situations. As of 2026, Apollo manages over $70 billion in market capitalization and is recognized as one of the largest asset managers globally.
ticker_apo.recent: In the past 30 days, Apollo reported earnings on May 6, 2026, with net income declining 68.2% year-over-year to $1.16 billion, though revenue grew 28.3% to $31.29 billion. The stock traded in a 52-week range of $99.56 to $157.28, closing at $127.79 on May 7, 2026. Analysts maintain a Buy rating with a price target of $147.27.

ticker_aapl.name: Apple Inc.
ticker_aapl.blurb: Apple designs and markets consumer electronics (iPhone, Mac, iPad, Apple Watch), software, and digital services. The iPhone remains the dominant revenue driver, but the Services segment — comprising the App Store, Apple Music, iCloud, Apple Pay, and licensing — has grown into a high-margin business that Wall Street values separately. Apple commands one of the highest brand loyalty rates in consumer technology and operates a tightly integrated hardware-software ecosystem.
ticker_aapl.recent: Apple reported FY2025 revenue of approximately $400 billion. The company has faced headwinds from slowing iPhone upgrade cycles in mature markets and regulatory pressure on App Store commissions in both the US and EU. Apple Intelligence, its generative AI suite, launched in late 2024 but has not yet materially re-accelerated upgrade cycles. Paul Pelosi sold 45,000 shares of AAPL according to the January 2026 PTR disclosure — the largest single sale in the filing by share count.

ticker_msft.name: Microsoft Corporation
ticker_msft.description: Microsoft is a global software, cloud, and AI platform company. Its principal segments are Productivity and Business Processes (Office, LinkedIn, Dynamics), Intelligent Cloud (Azure, server products), and More Personal Computing (Windows, Xbox, Surface). The company is in a structural transition from a capital-light software licensor to a capital-intensive hyperscale cloud and AI infrastructure provider.
ticker_msft.blurb: Microsoft is a global software, cloud, and AI platform company. Its principal segments are Productivity and Business Processes (Office, LinkedIn, Dynamics), Intelligent Cloud (Azure, server products), and More Personal Computing (Windows, Xbox, Surface). The company is in a structural transition from a capital-light software licensor to a capital-intensive hyperscale cloud and AI infrastructure provider.
ticker_msft.recent: As of early May 2026, MSFT trades near $413 — down approximately 25.6% from its July 31, 2025 all-time high of $555.45 and -15.7% YTD — after touching a March 28 correction low of $356.07. The drawdown carried the stock briefly below its 200-week moving average for the first time in roughly 13 years (prior touches: 2009, 2018, 2020, 2022). Revenue grew 18% YoY with Azure +40%, while annualized AI revenue reached approximately $37 billion; calendar-2026 capex is projected near $190 billion and free cash flow contracted -22% YoY. Forward P/E is approximately 24.4.

ticker_nvda.name: NVIDIA Corporation
ticker_nvda.blurb: NVIDIA designs graphics processing units (GPUs) and system-on-chip products. Originally a gaming chip company, it became the dominant supplier of AI accelerators — chips that perform the parallel matrix math required to train and run large language models. Its H100, H200, and Blackwell GPU families are the de facto standard for AI training infrastructure at hyperscalers and cloud providers. NVIDIA's CUDA software ecosystem creates deep switching costs: virtually all AI frameworks and models are optimised for CUDA, making competing hardware difficult to adopt at scale. NVIDIA also sells networking (InfiniBand, Ethernet) and data-centre systems.
ticker_nvda.recent: NVIDIA reported FY2026 (ending Jan 2026) revenue of $215.9 billion, up 65% YoY, with data centre revenue reaching $186 billion. The company's forward P/E of ~17.5x on 34.8% projected EPS growth produces a PEG of 0.50 — unusually cheap for what is arguably the most critical infrastructure company in the AI buildout. Hyperscalers (Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Meta) collectively committed over $200 billion in AI infrastructure capex for 2026, the majority flowing through NVIDIA's supply chain.

ticker_googl.name: Alphabet Inc. (Class A)
ticker_googl.blurb: Alphabet is the parent company of Google, the world's dominant search engine, as well as YouTube, the Google Cloud Platform, and a portfolio of moonshot bets (Waymo, DeepMind, Verily). Search advertising accounts for the majority of revenue, but the cloud division has grown into a multi-billion-dollar profit centre. Alphabet is also a leading player in generative AI, having developed the Gemini family of large language models and integrated them across its product suite.
ticker_googl.recent: Alphabet reported FY2025 revenue of approximately $370 billion, with Google Cloud crossing $50 billion annually. The company has faced antitrust scrutiny in both the US and EU, with a US federal court ruling in 2024 that Google holds an illegal monopoly in general search. Despite regulatory headwinds, the stock has benefited from AI-driven search enhancements and strong cloud growth. Paul Pelosi exercised call options with a $150 strike (purchased January 2025, exercised January 2026) gaining approximately 75% over the period.

sources.title: Nancy Pelosi's 2026 Stock Moves — Motley Fool

ticker_amzn.name: Amazon.com, Inc.
ticker_amzn.blurb: Amazon operates the world's largest e-commerce marketplace and the leading cloud infrastructure platform, Amazon Web Services (AWS). AWS generates the majority of Amazon's operating profit despite representing a minority of total revenue. The company also has significant positions in digital advertising, streaming (Prime Video), and logistics infrastructure. Amazon is a major investor in AI, both through AWS cloud AI services and through a multi-billion-dollar strategic stake in Anthropic.
ticker_amzn.recent: Amazon reported FY2025 revenue exceeding $650 billion, with AWS growing at roughly 17% annually and crossing $100 billion in run-rate revenue. The advertising segment has become a meaningful profit contributor. Paul Pelosi exercised call options with a $150 strike (purchased January 2025, exercised January 2026), with the stock gaining approximately 10% over that period — the weakest performer in the Pelosi 2026 exercise batch.

ticker_meta.name: Meta Platforms, Inc.
ticker_meta.blurb: Meta Platforms, headquartered in Menlo Park, California, operates Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Threads — collectively the largest social-media ecosystem in the world by monthly active users. The company generates the vast majority of its revenue through digital advertising, using detailed behavioural data to target ads across its platforms. After a painful 2022 in which shares fell roughly 65% amid a revenue slowdown and ballooning metaverse losses, Meta executed a dramatic turnaround by cutting costs, boosting margins, and rapidly integrating AI-driven ad ranking tools (Advantage+) that demonstrably improved advertiser returns. CEO Mark Zuckerberg declared 2023 a 'Year of Efficiency' and the company followed through. By late 2025 Meta was simultaneously the most profitable it had ever been and the most aggressive in AI infrastructure spending, committing up to $65 billion in capex for 2025 and raising that figure to as much as $145 billion for 2026.
ticker_meta.recent: Meta reached an all-time high near $796 per share in September 2025. The stock declined approximately 24–28% from that peak through April 2026, with the primary investor concern being the scale of the 2026 capital-expenditure commitment — up to $145 billion — and uncertainty about whether AI-driven revenue would materialise at the pace required to justify it. Quarterly earnings remained strong through the period, but multiple compression drove share-price weakness.

ticker_tsla.name: Tesla Inc.
ticker_tsla.blurb: Tesla designs and manufactures battery-electric vehicles, energy storage systems, and solar products. Founded in 2003 and taken public in June 2010 at seventeen dollars per share, it became one of the most spectacular long-term equity stories of the 2010s: every share from the IPO, adjusted for subsequent stock splits, would be worth roughly 6,500 dollars by late 2025 — a return of approximately 22,000 percent. The company's Model S (2012), Model 3 (2017), and Model Y (2020) progressively expanded the addressable market from luxury to mass-market segments. Tesla also operates a global Supercharger network and a large-scale energy storage division (Megapack). CEO Elon Musk's public profile — across social media, SpaceX, and his acquisition of X (formerly Twitter) — has made Tesla one of the more volatile large-cap equities in recent years, as investor sentiment toward the company has become partially indexed to sentiment toward Musk personally.
ticker_tsla.recent: Tesla has faced intensifying competition from Chinese electric-vehicle manufacturers, particularly BYD, which overtook Tesla in global EV sales in 2023. Revenue growth decelerated sharply in 2024, and the company has relied on price cuts to defend market share, compressing margins. Musk's political visibility during the 2024 US election cycle and his role in the DOGE cost-cutting initiative generated significant consumer backlash in some markets, with Tesla registrations declining in Europe and California in early 2025. The stock traded in a wide range through 2025-2026 as investors weighed the autonomous-vehicle (Full Self-Driving) optionality against near-term margin pressure.
